title: Constitutional Syscalls
description_html:
This paper introduces Constitutional Syscalls, a reframing of the system call interface as an explicit authority boundary governed by versioned contracts. Traditional operating systems treat syscalls as privileged traps into a kernel presumed to own execution reality, implicitly fusing mechanism (how an operation is performed) with jurisdiction (whether it is permitted). As execution environments become virtualized, sandboxed, replayable, and distributed, this fusion becomes unstable.

Constitutional Syscalls separates mechanism from jurisdiction by defining each system call as a typed request evaluated by an explicit admissibility function. Outcomes are first-class and structured: execute, simulate, defer, or refuse. Refusal is not an error but a legitimate constitutional outcome carrying machine-readable reason metadata. This shift transforms execution semantics from trap to adjudication.

The paper formalizes a minimal model with:

  • A Syscall structure including required authority and contract identifiers

  • An Authority structure with capabilities, policies, and a contract registry

  • An Admissibility : Syscall × Authority → Outcome × Reason function

  • A compositional model for multi-authority chains (e.g., replay engine → runtime → kernel)

  • A ConstitutionalLog structure enabling deterministic replay and auditable refusal

Graphical user interface (GUI) operations serve as a stress test, demonstrating how explicit authority contracts enable temporal portability across heterogeneous authorities, including kernels, WebAssembly runtimes, and replay engines. The model generalizes ideas from capability systems, reference monitors, microkernels (e.g., seL4), and WASI by making authority evaluation itself explicit, typed, and inspectable.

Constitutional Syscalls complements the broader Substrate Migration Principle by illustrating how authority evaluation can descend into execution substrate as an enforceable invariant. The result is an execution model in which legitimacy is explicit, refusal is accountable, and system interaction becomes governable across time and jurisdiction.
